title: Clean-to-Dirty Workflow, Tools, Surfaces & Personnel Movement

content.overview: Specialist instruction for clean-to-dirty workflow, tools, surfaces & personnel movement in propagation and clean-stock operations.

sections.title: Movement order is a control
sections.body: Workflows can reduce avoidable transfer by moving from lower-risk to higher-risk areas and by separating incoming, suspect and cleared material. Production urgency does not erase the contamination pathway.

sections.title: Sanitation must follow the validated procedure
sections.body: Tools, surfaces and reusable equipment require the facility-approved cleaning/disinfection and release process. A visibly clean surface is not evidence that the applicable sanitation procedure was completed.

sections.title: People carry workflow state too
sections.body: Hands, gloves, clothing, carts and shared implements can bridge zones. A specialist should design observable checkpoints for entry, exit, tool exchange and exception handling rather than rely on memory.

commonMistakes: Wiping a tool casually and treating it as validated sanitation.
Moving from suspect to clean stock because the task is urgent.
Relying on worker memory instead of visible workflow checkpoints.
content.practicalApplication: Design a propagation work sequence for clean, incoming, suspect and held stock that specifies movement order, tool exchange/sanitation checkpoints and stop conditions without naming unvalidated chemical recipes.
content.summary: Clean-to-dirty workflow is a controlled movement system; sanitation chemistry and exact procedures remain facility validated.
